reviews.review:
When I was ten hours into the game, I was willing to give it a glowing review, and I was puzzled by its mixed reception. Two days later, and I get it. 

Rue Valley is an adventure game which evokes Disco Elysium in presenting a story in a small town, accompanied by an inner monologue speaking to 'you' and a set of eclectic character traits that you select. Where traditional RPGs have you select a trait for 'strength' or 'magic', here you must select negative personality traits. The unique feature is the story is set in a time loop, and your character is a profoundly depressed, dysfunctional man  (actually, that is rather like Disco Elysium). 

As you explore the world, a small but mostly charming cast of characters unfolds before you, and there are plenty of fun moments where you take advantage of the time loop to gradually advance your understanding of the main events, as well as the back story of the people and places of Rue Valley.

So far, so good. Really good, in fact.  However, the last third or so of the game fumbles just about everything. 

To begin with, it eventually dawns that Rue Valley is playing a shell game when it comes to choice and reactivity. None of the points in your traits matter. You have a bunch of moments where the game makes a big show of testing whether you might progress on a puzzle based on these, but my character failed every single one, and they don't open up new avenues. 

There is a lengthy sequence where the relatively open nature of the exploration is effectively taken from the player, and you are railroaded into actions that feel inconsistent with what either the player or the protagonist would do—there were many alternatives available!

Soon, there was an [i]extensive[/i] montage sequence where the character searches for something crucial, but after searching everywhere, they are forced to give up and have another mental breakdown. Cue an even longer on-rails segment that only relents when the character finally discovers what they have been looking for right under their nose the whole time.

Thematically, this makes sense. However, in practice it makes no sense considering that the character was literally looking for a place which was in sight of the locations we have been tramping back and forth from the whole game. What's worse, even if this place was not visible, it would logically be the first place anyone would start looking. This sequence was supposed to be transformative for the protagonist, but for me it had the opposite effect. This was where I mentally gave up on the game. 

Although I am sympathetic to the concept of a game where much of the conflict is driven by a character's inner turmoil (I loved Disco Elysium after all), it wore me down eventually in this case. The protagonist is such a sad sack, and his dialogue options so frequently compel us to take actions that were impulsive, childish, or pathetic. Disco Elysium provided the option for its detective protagonist to learn and grow—or fail miserably, depending on your choices (okay, last reference to that title). We see things from another perspective occasionally in Rue Valley, but this other perspective is deranged to the point of dissociation. 

Finally, and worst of all, the game leaves so many of its interesting threads unfinished. Virtually all of the characters feel like they don't have a resolution, and the protagonist is one of them, unfortunately. [spoiler]Even the central mystery of the time loop goes completely unanswered![/spoiler]

It pains me to give this game a thumbs down. Rue Valley starts out quite strong, only to lose its way near the end.
reviews.developer_response:
Hello!
We’ve already been digging in the exact areas of the game you mentioned, and the team is currently working on improving the game’s ending, expanding the pool of interactive objects, and reviewing the clarity of status effects and inspiration points. 
Thanks for your detailed feedback, it really helps us see where the experience drags and where it shines.
